t: The provisions of the final paragraph of section 10 of the Railway Labor Act (45 U.S.C. 160), as heretofore extended by law, shall be hereby reinstated and extended until 12:01 o’clock ante-meridian of the ninety-first day after enactment of this resolution with respect to the dispute referred to in Executive Order 11324, January 28, 1967.

fable.w: The tempting reading is that a reference to the Railway Labor Act and a labor dispute (carriers and unions, an emergency board) implies outside parties taking part in a federal decision. But this section only reinstates and extends the statutory status-quo period for a specific dispute. It creates no comment period, hearing, advisory body, consultation requirement, or right to sue involving any non-federal party.
fable.s: shall be hereby reinstated and extended until 12:01 o’clock ante-meridian of the ninety-first day after enactment of this resolution with respect to the dispute referred to in Executive Order 11324

qwen_block.w: This section merely extends the duration of a legal provision regarding a labor dispute. It does not establish any mechanism for outside parties (such as the public, states, or experts) to consult with, advise, or participate in a federal decision-making process. The text describes a legislative action to reinstate a statute, not a participatory process.
qwen_block.s: The provisions of the final paragraph of section 10 of the Railway Labor Act (45 U.S.C. 160), as heretofore extended by law, shall be hereby reinstated and extended until 12:01 o’clock ante-meridian of the ninety-first day after enactment of this resolution with respect to the dispute referred to in Executive Order 11324, January 28, 1967.

opus.w: This resolution only extends the status-quo (cooling-off) period in the final paragraph of section 10. During that period, the parties to a rail labor dispute may not change working conditions. It does not require the federal government to consult outside parties before a decision. It also creates no advisory board, hearing, comment period or right to sue. The mention of section 10, where emergency boards are set up, is tempting, but this resolution does not invoke or create any board process. It only freezes the parties' conduct.
opus.s: The provisions of the final paragraph of section 10 of the Railway Labor Act (45 U.S.C. 160), as heretofore extended by law, shall be hereby reinstated and extended until 12:01 o’clock ante-meridian of the ninety-first day after enactment of this resolution

qwen_chat.w: This section merely extends the time limit for a dispute resolution process under the Railway Labor Act. It does not establish a new advisory body, require public comment, or mandate consultation with outside parties. The extension of a statutory deadline is an internal procedural adjustment, not a form of public participation.
qwen_chat.s: The provisions of the final paragraph of section 10 of the Railway Labor Act (45 U.S.C. 160), as heretofore extended by law, shall be hereby reinstated and extended until 12:01 o’clock ante-meridian of the ninety-first day after enactment of this resolution with respect to the dispute referred to in Executive Order 11324, January 28, 1967.
qwen_chat.b: Tempting-but-wrong reading: One might think that extending the Railway Labor Act provisions implies a continuation of mediation or arbitration processes involving outside parties (like a National Railroad Adjustment Board or mediators). However, the text itself only extends a statutory deadline for a specific dispute resolution process; it does not explicitly describe a mechanism for public participation, consultation with non-federal entities, or advisory committees in this specific section. The section is purely procedural regarding the timeline of an existing legal framework.
